The cheapest dominating set found is 1, 4, and 6 (accent), with an accent edge from each other node to the member that dominates it. The card shows [1, 4, 6] and total weight 1 + 1 + 1 = 3." width="100%"} A dominating set is a set of nodes such that every node in the graph is either in the set or adjacent to a member. When nodes have a cost (a weight), the goal is a dominating set with the smallest total cost rather than the fewest nodes. Finding the exact optimum is NP-hard, so this method uses a greedy algorithm: at each step it adds the node with the lowest weight per newly covered node (the node itself plus its not-yet-covered neighbors), and stops once every node is covered. This provides an `O(log n)` approximation to the optimal solution. Typical uses are coverage and placement problems where locations have different costs: - placing facilities, cell towers, or sensors so that every site is served by one located at it or next door - choosing a cheap set of monitors or "seed" nodes that touch the whole network - selecting a small set of representatives, weighted by how costly each one is to use Without `node_weight_attr=`, every node costs `1` and the method becomes the classic greedy heuristic for a small (unweighted) dominating set, repeatedly picking the node that covers the most uncovered nodes. Ties are broken in favor of the smaller node ID, so the result is deterministic. The method is intended for undirected graphs: on a directed graph, a chosen node covers only itself and its out-neighbors. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute holding each node's cost. If `None` (the default), every node has weight `1`. If given, nodes where the attribute is missing or cannot be converted to a float are assigned weight `1`. Lower weights make a node more attractive to include; use non-negative values. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs forming an approximate minimum weighted dominating set, sorted in ascending order. An empty graph gives an empty list. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Implements the Chvátal-style greedy heuristic that at each step picks the node minimizing *weight per newly dominated node*: the candidate's weight divided by the number of uncovered nodes in its closed neighborhood. Each step scans all remaining candidates, so the cost is roughly $O(V \cdot (V + E))$ in the worst case. The result is a dominating set whose total weight is within an $O(\log n)$ factor of optimal, a bound that matches the best possible polynomial-time approximation ratio for the weighted set-cover problem it generalizes. Nodes with a missing or unrecognized `node_weight_attr=` attribute are treated as weight $1$. Note that `dominating_set()` uses a different, faster heuristic that does not aim to minimize size, so the two methods can return different sets even when all weights are $1$. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The hub costs far more than any leaf, so the weighted algorithm favors dominating via the cheaper leaves (total cost 3) rather than picking the hub (cost 10): ::: {#aaabd691 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="hub", cost=10) .add_nodes(["leaf1", "leaf2", "leaf3"], cost=1) .add_edges([("hub", "leaf1"), ("hub", "leaf2"), ("hub", "leaf3")]) ) dom = graph.minimum_weighted_dominating_set(node_weight_attr="cost") # Returns the labels chosen to minimize total cost [graph.get_label_from_id(n) for n in dom] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['leaf1', 'leaf2', 'leaf3'] ``` ::: ::: Ignoring the costs (every node weighs 1) changes the answer: the hub alone covers all four nodes, so it is the cheapest choice: ::: {#eb013e40 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} [graph.get_label_from_id(n) for n in graph.minimum_weighted_dominating_set()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['hub'] ``` ::: ::: This generalizes to a facility-location-style problem: place facilities at low-cost nodes such that every node in the grid is covered: ::: {#b30b2533 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import random graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_grid_2d(rows=5, cols=5) random.seed(23) node_ids = graph.get_node_ids() costs = {nid: random.uniform(1, 10) for nid in node_ids} graph.set_node_attrs("facility_cost", costs) facilities = graph.minimum_weighted_dominating_set(node_weight_attr="facility_cost") # (number of facilities, whether they cover the whole grid) (len(facilities), graph.is_dominating_set(facilities)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (8, True) ``` ::: :::
